questions.stem: Which one of the following is not an example of divide and conquer algorithm?
questions.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
sources: MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 65

answer.text: Heap sort
answer.explanation: DAA16 explicitly classifies heap sort as outside standard divide and conquer: it builds a heap and repeatedly extracts its maximum. Quicksort partitions and recursively sorts ranges; merge sort recursively sorts halves; binary search recursively or iteratively reduces to a smaller half. Thus heap sort is the single exclusion among the listed algorithms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quicksort partitions its input and recursively sorts the resulting smaller ranges, a standard divide-and-conquer pattern.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search repeatedly reduces a sorted search interval to one half; the note treats this as divide-and-conquer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort divides into halves, sorts each recursively, and combines them by merging.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly restores it after extraction, rather than independently sorting and combining subinstances.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer solves smaller largely independent instances and combines results. DP reuses a defined set of subproblem states. Greedy commits to a feasible local choice only when a safety argument supports it. Backtracking grows/retracts candidates when constraints fail; branch and bound also rejects candidates whose best possible objective cannot beat an incumbent.

Heap sort builds a max-heap in Θ(n), then extracts/restores in O(log n) per item: O(n log n) total, Θ(1) auxiliary space, ordinarily unstable. It is not standard D&C. Merge sort offers stability/worst-case guarantees; quicksort’s practical advantage depends on implementation/workload.

This rearranging is referred to as partitioning.

answer.text: Θ(log n)
answer.explanation: The loop visits i=1,2,4,… while i<n, so it executes ceil(log₂n) iterations. Each iteration has constant work under the stated arithmetic and output model, and initialization, the fixed prompt and return add constant overhead. The total is therefore Θ(log n).

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic grows faster and is not the tight order.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The doubling loop takes logarithmically many constant-cost iterations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linear is a looser upper bound rather than the tight order.

evidence.quote: Sequential costs add; independent nested loop counts multiply. A dependent loop requires summation. n iterations of a constant body give Θ(n); ∑i=1.. n i=n(n+1)/2 gives Θ(n²). answer.text: Smaller instances of the same problem
answer.explanation: Recursion reduces a problem to simpler instances of that same problem (PDF p.14). Thus smaller same-problem instances, with a terminating base case, match the definition.

choices.explanation: Larger instances do not implement the reducing step on p.14.

choices.label: B

If an optimal solution can be created for a problem by constructing optimal solutions for
its subproblems, the problem possesses property.
questions.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 77

answer.text: Optimal substructure
answer.explanation: Optimal substructure means an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems (PDF p.28). The principle of optimality on p.49 expresses exactly the construction in the stem.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Overlap concerns repeated subproblems, not optimality of their solutions (pp.28,49).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the named property defined on p.28.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memoization stores computed answers; it is not the optimality property (p.49).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Greedy is a design strategy requiring additional choice conditions (p.28).

evidence.quote: Define state meaning, choices, recurrence, bases and dependency order. Prove replacing a subsolution by a better one improves the full solution; otherwise state information may be missing. Show the recurrence covers all legal final choices and generates feasible candidates, then induct in dependency order. Store choices for reconstruction.

A greedy algorithm repeatedly selects a locally attractive feasible option without later undoing it. Optimal substructure alone does not prove this safe. An exchange proof inserts the greedy choice into an optimum without worsening cost; recurse. MST cut proofs use this exchange.

If a problem can be broken into subproblems that are reused several times, the problem
possesses property.
questions.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
sources: Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 78

answer.text: Overlapping subproblems
answer.explanation: Reusing a subproblem several times means subproblems share sub-subproblems, the contrast made on PDF p.48. This is overlapping subproblems; storing an answer is a response to that property, not the property itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Shared sub-subproblems and repeated work are described on p.48.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimal substructure concerns optimal solutions rather than repetition (p.28).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Saving results in a table addresses repeated work; it is not the reuse property (p.48).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A greedy choice is unrelated to whether subproblems recur (pp.28,48).

evidence.quote: Overlapping states motivate reuse; optimal substructure supports optimization. These are textbook signatures, not requirements that every DP problem optimize or every state have multiple users. DP also counts/decides. Cost=states×work per state and can remain exponential.

Memoization recursively checks a cache before solving a state and stores its result. Tabulation orders dependencies explicitly; chosen domains may exclude irrelevant states. Cache keys include all relevant parameters; recursion/locality/sparsity affect implementation cost.

module_refs.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms module
module_refs.quote: Dynamic programming, like the divide-and-conquer method, solves problems by combining the solutions to subproblems. As we saw in Chapter 2 of binary search, divide-and-conquer algorithms partition the problem into independent subproblems, solve the subproblems recursively, and then combine their solutions to solve the original problem. In contrast, dynamic programming is applicable when the subproblems are not independent, that is, when subproblems share sub subproblems. In this context, a divide-and-conquer algorithm does more work than necessary, repeatedly solving the common sub subproblems. A dynamic-programming algorithm solves every subproblem just once and then saves its answer in a table, thereby avoiding the work of recomputing the answer every time the subproblem is encountered. Dynamic programming is typically applied to optimization problems. In such problems there can be many possible solutions. Each solution has a value, and we wish to find a solution with the optimal (minimum or maximum) value.

questions.stem: For the standard Floyd–Warshall implementation on an n-vertex weighted graph, using constant-time distance arithmetic and the full k,i,j loops, what is the tight running-time bound?
questions.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
sources: Computer Science model exam · Question 16
University of Gondar model exam · Question 16

answer.text: Θ(n³)
answer.explanation: Floyd–Warshall considers each intermediate vertex k and updates every ordered pair i,j. The three independent n-sized loop ranges perform Θ(n³) constant-cost updates. The n² output table explains storage, not the time of this implementation. Other graph assumptions can support different algorithms, so this is the cost of the explicitly named method rather than a universal best-achievable APSP bound.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quadratic counts pair storage but misses the intermediate-vertex loop.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Three full n-sized loops give cubic time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear is too small even for the explicit pair table.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Quartic is a loose upper bound rather than the tight cost.

evidence.quote: For all-pairs distances initialize D[i, i]=0, D[i, j] to the minimum direct edge weight, and missing edges to∞. Preserve a negative self-loop by taking min(0, its weight). For k outermost, update D[i, j]=min(D[i, j], D[i, k]+D[k, j]); before phase k, intermediates are restricted to earlier vertices. Guard unreachable sums and numeric overflow.

Three loops give Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) storage. A negative diagonal afterward identifies a negative cycle; pairs able to traverse it have no finite minimum walk distance. Warshall reachability replaces min/+ by OR/AND. Floyd’s cost is not a universal best-achievable bound for all APSP settings; sparse nonnegative graphs permit repeated Dijkstra and other models permit other methods.

questions.hint: Identify the specification and cost model, then apply the relevant bound, invariant or strategy rule.
sources: Computer Science model exam · Question 26
University of Gondar model exam · Question 26

answer.text: Merge sort
answer.explanation: DAA14 splits into halves, recursively sorts each, and merges the results, directly implementing divide and conquer. DAA16 excludes standard heap sort from that category and describes selection’s repeated minimum and bubble’s adjacent passes. Only Merge Sort among these options has the specified independent recursive decomposition and combination mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Merge sort recursively solves halves and combines them through a merge.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Standard heapsort builds and repeatedly restores a heap rather than applying the standard independent-subproblem decomposition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Selection repeatedly finds a suffix minimum instead of recursively sorting halves.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Bubble repeatedly swaps adjacent inversions instead of recursively decomposing subinstances.

evidence.quote: Split by indices, recursively sort each half, then repeatedly copy the smaller remaining front element into a temporary result. The merge invariant says the output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest elements already consumed. Append the unexhausted suffix. Equal keys must be taken from the left half first to preserve stability.

Insertion shifts larger sorted-prefix keys: stable with strict comparisons, Θ(n) best and Θ(n²) worst. Optimized bubble sort swaps adjacent inversions and stops after a no-swap pass: stable, Θ(n) best, Θ(n²) worst. Selection repeatedly finds a suffix minimum: Θ(n²) comparisons in every order, normally unstable. These use Θ(1) auxiliary array space.

module_refs.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms module
module_refs.quote: Dynamic programming, like the divide-and-conquer method, solves problems by combining the solutions to subproblems. As we saw in Chapter 2 of binary search, divide-and-conquer algorithms partition the problem into independent subproblems, solve the subproblems recursively, and then combine their solutions to solve the original problem. In contrast, dynamic programming is applicable when the subproblems are not independent, that is, when subproblems share sub subproblems. In this context, a divide-and-conquer algorithm does more work than necessary, repeatedly solving the common sub subproblems. A dynamic-programming algorithm solves every subproblem just once and then saves its answer in a table, thereby avoiding the work of recomputing the answer every time the subproblem is encountered. Dynamic programming is typically applied to optimization problems. In such problems there can be many possible solutions. Each solution has a value, and we wish to find a solution with the optimal (minimum or maximum) value.

module_refs.quote: Dynamic programming, like the divide-and-conquer method, solves problems by combining the solutions to subproblems. As we saw in Chapter 2 of binary search, divide-and-conquer algorithms partition the problem into independent subproblems, solve the subproblems recursively, and then combine their solutions to solve the original problem. In contrast, dynamic programming is applicable when the subproblems are not independent, that is, when subproblems share sub subproblems. A dynamic-programming algorithm solves every subproblem just once and then saves its answer in a table, thereby avoiding the work of recomputing the answer every time the subproblem is encountered. Dynamic programming is typically applied to optimization problems. In such problems there can be many possible solutions. answer.text: Naive recursion repeats Fibonacci states; DP computes each required state once.
answer.explanation: DAA26 shows that F(n−2) reappears across recursion branches, causing Θ(φ^n) calls, with O(2^n) a valid loose bound. questions.stem: What is the 0/1 knapsack optimization problem with positive integer weights, nonnegative values and integer capacity W, and why does its item-and-capacity state formulation suit dynamic programming? Each item may be chosen at most once.

sources: Algorithm Design & Analysis review questions · Question 37

answer.text: Choose a subset with total weight at most W and maximum total value. DP compares excluding each item with including it once and reuses item/capacity state results.
answer.explanation: Define K[i,w] as the best value using the first i items within capacity w. An item that fits can be excluded or included with its value added to K[i-1,w-weight_i]; taking the larger value gives the recurrence. The previous-row reference enforces at-most-once use, and repeated states are reused. The O(nW) running time is pseudo-polynomial in binary-encoded capacity, unlike the separate fractional-knapsack greedy method.

evidence.quote: For integer capacity W, K[i, w] is maximum value using the first i items within capacity w. Initialize K[0, w]=0. If weight_i>w, use K[i−1, w]; otherwise take max(K[i−1, w], value_i+K[i−1, w−weight_i]). The previous-row reference ensures each item is used at most once. Backtrack changed values to recover chosen items.

This proof depends on divisibility. With capacity 10 and items(6,12),(5,8),(5,8), ratio-greedy chooses value 12; the two weight 5 items give 16 under 0/1 rules. Specify whether the knapsack problem is fractional,0/1 or unbounded. Feasibility alone does not guarantee optimality.

answer.text: APSP finds shortest distances for every ordered vertex pair; Floyd–Warshall is one DP algorithm.
answer.explanation: DAA28 initializes direct-edge costs and progressively allows each vertex as an intermediate. Its min-plus recurrence gives Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) storage. Negative cycles make affected pair distances lack a finite minimum; Floyd detects them through negative diagonals. Its cost is a taught solution rather than a universal best-achievable APSP bound.

evidence.quote: For all-pairs distances initialize D[i, i]=0, D[i, j] to the minimum direct edge weight, and missing edges to∞. Preserve a negative self-loop by taking min(0, its weight). For k outermost, update D[i, j]=min(D[i, j], D[i, k]+D[k, j]); before phase k, intermediates are restricted to earlier vertices. Guard unreachable sums and numeric overflow.

Three loops give Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) storage. A negative diagonal afterward identifies a negative cycle; pairs able to traverse it have no finite minimum walk distance. Warshall reachability replaces min/+ by OR/AND. Floyd’s cost is not a universal best-achievable bound for all APSP settings; sparse nonnegative graphs permit repeated Dijkstra and other models permit other methods.

answer.text: A locally attractive choice can block the optimum; coins {1,3,4} for target 6 are a counterexample.
answer.explanation: DAA19’s largest-first choice produces 4+1+1, using three coins, while 3+3 uses two. questions.stem: For ordinary array quicksort, what partition pattern causes quadratic worst-case time, and how can randomized pivot selection or three-way partitioning mitigate relevant workloads? Distinguish expected-time improvements from worst-case and stack-space guarantees.

answer.text: Repeated very unbalanced partitions cause quadratic work. Random pivots give expected Theta(n log n) time; three-way partitioning helps repeated keys, and smaller-side recursion can limit stack space.
answer.explanation: Extreme pivots can leave subproblems of sizes n-1,n-2 and so on, giving quadratic total partition work. Random pivots improve expected time to Theta(n log n) but do not remove quadratic possible executions. Three-way partitioning helps repeated keys, while median-of-three still admits adversarial inputs. Recursing only on the smaller side and iterating on the larger separately bounds stack depth by O(log n). No universal rarity claim is needed.

evidence.quote: Balanced splits give Θ(n log n); repeatedly highly unbalanced splits give Θ(n²). Random pivots give expected Θ(n log n), not a deterministic guarantee. Median-of-three does not eliminate adversarial cases; three-way partitioning helps repeated keys. Standard quicksort is unstable, uses expected Θ(log n) stack but worst Θ(n); recursing on the smaller side and iterating on the larger bounds stack by O(log n).

questions.stem: Using the note’s worst-case bounds, compare matrix-based Prim with Kruskal that comparison-sorts all edges on a dense simple undirected graph, where E=Theta(V²). Why can this implementation pairing favor Prim asymptotically?

answer.text: Matrix Prim has O(V²) time; edge-sorting Kruskal has O(E log E)=O(V² log V). The matrix implementation avoids the all-edge sorting factor.
answer.explanation: The matrix-based Prim implementation scans vertex connections in O(V²) time. Kruskal’s stated bound includes sorting all E edges, giving O(E log E). For dense simple graphs E has order V², so that expression becomes O(V² log V), whereas matrix Prim retains its quadratic bound. This explains the advantage of the specified implementations and does not claim that every version of Prim is always faster in measured runtime.

evidence.quote: Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Kruskal sorts edges globally, accepting one only when union-find says its endpoints are in different components. The cut proof exchanges a light crossing edge into some optimum without raising its weight. Matrix Prim costs O(V²); binary-heap Prim O(E log V), and Kruskal O(E log E). Dense-graph comparisons depend on these implementations. Disconnected input gives a minimum spanning forest.

answer.text: Standard Dijkstra is not generally correct with negative edges.

Some instances may happen to work, but no general guarantee remains. Bellman–Ford or DAG DP supplies an appropriate alternative under its assumptions.

evidence.quote: Nonnegative edges ensure a later path through unsettled vertices cannot improve a finalized distance. With s→a=2, s→b=5, b→a=−4, finalizing a at 2 misses the later distance 1. Binary-heap/list implementation costs O((V+E)log V), matrix scanning O(V²). An MST minimizes total connection cost; Dijkstra minimizes each source-path distance, a different objective.

For a general graph, Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges for up to V−1 passes and tests an additional pass for a reachable negative cycle: O(VE). Thus “single-source shortest path” does not uniquely imply greedy; graph assumptions determine the algorithm.

answer.text: Both repeatedly combine the two smallest weights; Huffman interprets the resulting tree as a prefix code.
answer.explanation: DAA22 uses file sizes as merge weights and frequencies as Huffman weights. Reinsert each combined weight so large values avoid unnecessary depth. In Huffman the weighted path length is ∑frequency×depth, the same merge-tree objective. Equal-weight choices can change codewords without changing the optimal total cost.

evidence.quote: Combine the two smallest weights, add their sum to total cost, and reinsert it. A min-heap gives O(n log n) time/O(n) space. Cost p+q counts moved records; worst-case comparisons are p+q−1 for nonempty lists, and actual comparisons may be fewer.

Huffman uses frequencies as weights and 0/1 branches to leaf symbols, making a prefix-free code. Cost is∑frequency×depth. An exchange makes the two least frequencies deepest siblings; contract them and induct. Ties can change codes without changing optimal cost. Header overhead can outweigh tiny-file savings.

notes.title: TSP branch and bound by matrix reduction

blocks.text: For directed TSP, set diagonal/forbidden entries to∞.
Subtract each finite row minimum, then each finite column minimum, accumulating reductions.
Every tour uses one entry per row/column, so their sum is a lower bound; the relaxed assignment may contain disjoint subtours.
When including edge i→j, remove its used row/column, prevent premature subtours, reduce again and add the selected reduced-edge cost and new reductions to the parent bound.
Compare bounds with the best complete tour and expand a promising live node.
Never treat a reduced matrix’s zeros as proof of a complete valid tour.
Branch on an undecided edge i->j. The include child deletes row i/column j and adds its selected reduced cost plus new reductions to the parent bound.
The exclude child sets that entry to infinity and adds only new reductions.
Keep forced in/out-degree at most one.
Track each forced path from head h to tail t and forbid t->h until the path contains every vertex; this blocks premature cycles.
A required residual row/column with no finite choice is infeasible and pruned.
Accept only one complete cycle through every vertex, not a set of disjoint cycles.

notes.title: P, NP, reductions and encoding size

blocks.text: P contains decision problems solvable deterministically in polynomial input-bit time.
NP contains decision problems with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine.
NP does not mean non-polynomial; P⊆NP.
Whether P=NP remains open.
A polynomial many-one reduction A≤p B transforms each A-instance into a B-instance preserving yes/no. To prove B NP-hard, reduce a known hard A to B, not the reverse.
NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP; optimization TSP is normally called NP-hard, while its bounded-tour decision form is NP-complete.
A valid proposed tour and its cost are easy to check, but certifying global optimality is another task.
Pseudo-polynomial O(nW) knapsack is not polynomial in the bit length of W.
